message.content:
The number of distinct positions that can arise in a legal game of chess is astronomically large.  In fact, the best estimates put it at roughly

\[
10^{43}\text{–}10^{50}
\]

legal positions.  The classic “Shannon number” for chess is about \(10^{43}\) positions, but more recent analyses suggest the true figure may be closer to \(10^{46}\) or even \(10^{47}\).

If you’re asking about the number of possible *games* (i.e., sequences of legal moves from the starting position to any end state), the estimate is even larger—on the order of \(10^{120}\) distinct games.  This is sometimes called the “game-tree complexity” of chess.

So, in short:

| Quantity | Rough estimate |
|----------|----------------|
| Legal positions | \(10^{43}\)–\(10^{50}\) |
| Possible games | \(\approx 10^{120}\) |

These figures illustrate why exhaustive search of all possible chess positions or games is computationally infeasible.

But the question might be ambiguous: "total number of possible arrangements in a chess game" could refer to the number of possible games (sequences of moves). That is about 10^120. But likely they want the number of possible positions: about 10^43. The known estimate: 10^43 to 10^50. The Shannon number: 10^43. The more precise estimate: 10^46.
